::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
- Animate any property with a tween and an ease.
- Use timers and delayed calls.
- Emit particles, once and continuously.
- Add camera shake and hit-stop, and know when to stop.

## Same game, different feel

Play this with everything switched on, then switch things off one at a time. The rules don't change at all.

{{< game stopping-points/stopE id="feel-game" caption="Pick up a sample, get hit by a cart, store it. Then switch things off." >}}

{{< tuning target="feel-game" switches="feel.tweens, feel.particles, feel.shake" sliders="feel.hitStopMs:0:300:10" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
With everything off, *Cold Chain* still works, and it's noticeably worse. Getting hit feels like nothing happened. Storing a sample feels like ticking a box. Designers call this **game feel**, or **juice**: small, fast, physical responses that make actions feel like they matter.

Almost all of it is built from four tools: tweens, timers, particles and the camera.
:::

## Tweens

A **tween** changes a property smoothly, from where it is to where you say, over a duration.

```js
this.tweens.add({
  targets: this.carried,     // any game object, or a list of them
  scale: { from: 1.8, to: 1 }, // any numeric property: x, y, alpha, angle, scale...
  duration: 250,             // milliseconds
  ease: 'Back.Out',          // how it gets there
});
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
That's the pop when you pick up a sample: the tube appears big and settles to its normal size. A few more options cover most uses:

- `yoyo: true` plays it forwards, then backwards.
- `repeat: -1` loops forever (with `yoyo`, a pulse).
- `delay: 200` waits before starting.
- `onComplete: () => ...` runs when it's done.

Tweens work on *any* numeric property of *any* object, including your own: `this.tweens.add({ targets: this, thaw: 0, duration: 500 })` would drain the thaw meter smoothly.
:::

## Eases

An **ease** decides *how* a tween travels: steady, fast then slow, overshooting, bouncing.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ease = Inputs.radio(["Linear", "Quad.Out", "Cubic.Out", "Back.Out", "Bounce.Out", "Elastic.Out", "Sine.InOut"], {value: "Back.Out", label: "ease"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
easeFns = ({
  "Linear": t => t,
  "Quad.Out": t => 1 - (1 - t) * (1 - t),
  "Cubic.Out": t => 1 - Math.pow(1 - t, 3),
  "Back.Out": t => { const s = 1.70158; return 1 + (s + 1) * Math.pow(t - 1, 3) + s * Math.pow(t - 1, 2); },
  "Bounce.Out": t => {
    const n = 7.5625, d = 2.75;
    if (t < 1 / d) return n * t * t;
    if (t < 2 / d) return n * (t -= 1.5 / d) * t + 0.75;
    if (t < 2.5 / d) return n * (t -= 2.25 / d) * t + 0.9375;
    return n * (t -= 2.625 / d) * t + 0.984375;
  },
  "Elastic.Out": t => t === 0 || t === 1 ? t : Math.pow(2, -10 * t) * Math.sin((t * 10 - 0.75) * (2 * Math.PI) / 3) + 1,
  "Sine.InOut": t => -(Math.cos(Math.PI * t) - 1) / 2,
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const f = easeFns[ease];
  const W = 640, H = 300, pad = 40;
  const x = t => pad + t * (W - 2 * pad);
  const y = v => H - pad - v * (H - 2.6 * pad);
  const pts = d3.range(0, 1.0001, 0.01).map(t => [x(t), y(f(t))]);
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("max-width", "640px")
    .style("background", "#d8dee6").style("border-radius", "6px");
  svg.append("line").attr("x1", x(0)).attr("x2", x(1)).attr("y1", y(1)).attr("y2", y(1))
    .attr("stroke", "#94a3b8").attr("stroke-dasharray", "4 4");
  svg.append("line").attr("x1", x(0)).attr("x2", x(1)).attr("y1", y(0)).attr("y2", y(0)).attr("stroke", "#94a3b8");
  svg.append("path").attr("d", d3.line()(pts)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#0e7490").attr("stroke-width", 4);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", x(0)).attr("y", H - 12).attr("font-family", "monospace").attr("font-size", 14).text("start");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", x(1) - 30).attr("y", H - 12).attr("font-family", "monospace").attr("font-size", 14).text("end");
  const dot = svg.append("circle").attr("r", 9).attr("fill", "#dc2626");
  const box = svg.append("rect").attr("x", W - 28).attr("width", 16).attr("height", 16).attr("fill", "#0e7490");
  const node = svg.node();
  let start = performance.now();
  (function frame(now) {
    if (!node.isConnected && performance.now() - start > 2000) return;
    const t = ((now - start) % 1600) / 1200;
    const p = Math.min(t, 1);
    dot.attr("cx", x(p)).attr("cy", y(f(p)));
    box.attr("y", y(f(p)) - 8);
    requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  })(start);
  return node;
}
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The curve shows progress (up) against time (along). The square on the right moves the way an object would.

- **`.Out`** eases start fast and slow down at the end. They feel *responsive*, so they're the default for anything the player caused.
- **`.In`** eases start slow and speed up: things falling, leaving, being sucked away.
- **`Back.Out`** overshoots a little and settles: a pop, a bounce of life. *Cold Chain*'s pickup.
- **`Linear`** feels mechanical. Good for timers and progress bars, odd for anything physical.
:::

## Timers

```js
this.time.delayedCall(450, () => this.freezer.setFrame(0));   // once, later

this.time.addEvent({ delay: 1000, loop: true, callback: () => this.tick() }); // every second
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Use the scene's clock (`this.time`), not `setTimeout`. Scene timers pause when the scene pauses, stop when it stops, and run on game time. A `setTimeout` keeps going after the player pauses, and fires into a scene that may no longer exist.
:::

## Particles

A **particle emitter** spawns lots of short-lived images: frost, sparks, dust, smoke.

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/src/scenes/Play.js" lines="86-103" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Two emitters, two ways of using them:

- The **trail** is continuous. It follows the researcher (`startFollow`) and emits one frost flake every 80 ms. `start()` when you pick up a sample, `stop()` when you store it.
- The **burst** never emits on its own (`emitting: false`). `this.burst.explode(24, x, y)` throws 24 flakes out at once, at the freezer or the dry ice.

Values like `{ min: 5, max: 30 }` pick a random number for each particle; `{ start: 0.9, end: 0 }` changes it over the particle's life. Random and changing is what makes particles look natural.
:::

## The camera

```js
this.cameras.main.shake(140, 0.006);    // duration, intensity
this.cameras.main.flash(150, 255, 80, 80); // duration, red, green, blue
this.cameras.main.fadeOut(500);         // and fadeIn: between floors
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Shake intensity is a fraction of the screen size: 0.006 is gentle, 0.02 is violent. Keep it short. Long shakes are tiring and, for some people, nauseating.
:::

## Getting hit

All of it together, in one collision:

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/src/scenes/Play.js" method="bump" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Knockback**: you're thrown away from the cart, so the hit has a direction.
- **Sound** and a red **tint**, cleared after 150 ms.
- **Shake**, if switched on.
- **Hit-stop**: the physics freezes for 70 ms. You barely notice it consciously, but it makes impacts feel heavy, as if the game flinched. Fighting games are built on it.
- **Blinking**: a tween on `alpha` while you can't be hit again, so you know you're safe for a moment.

Every one of those is a response to the player's question "what just happened?".
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Phaser 3 habit" .phaser3}
Phaser 3 tutorials flash a hit sprite white with `sprite.setTintFill(0xffffff)`. In Phaser 4 that method still exists but does nothing. Use `sprite.setTint(0xffffff).setTintMode(Phaser.TintModes.FILL)`, and `clearTint()` to undo it.
:::

## Words that move

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopE/src/scenes/Play.js" method="floatText" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
"2 / 3" floating up from the freezer, "COLDER" from the dry ice, "THAWED" when you lose. A text, a tween up and out, and `destroy()` when it's done so you don't leave thousands of invisible texts behind.
:::

## When to stop

- **Feedback should match importance.** Storing a sample gets a shake; picking one up doesn't.
- **Never hide information.** Particles behind the HUD, a shake while you're trying to aim: juice that gets in the way is worse than none.
- **Let people turn it down.** Screen shake and flashing can make people unwell. A setting to switch them off (like `tuning.feel`) is cheap and kind.

A labmate wanted the thaw meter to pulse when it's nearly full. After a few seconds of danger, the meter flickers wildly and the game slows to a crawl. Their HUD code:

```js
redraw() {
  // ...
  if (thaw >= 75) {
    this.tweens.add({ targets: this.bar, alpha: 0.35, duration: 180, yoyo: true, repeat: -1 });
  }
}
```

[Answer](../answers/09-feel-answers.qmd#ex-9.3)
:::

## Key points

- Game feel is fast, physical feedback. It doesn't change the rules, but it changes everything.
- A tween animates any number, with an ease. `.Out` eases feel responsive.
- Use the scene clock (`this.time`), not `setTimeout`.
- Particle emitters run continuously (`start`, `stop`) or in bursts (`explode`).
- Shake, flash and hit-stop make impacts land. Match them to importance, and let players turn them off.
